Biodiversity is declining worldwide due to anthropogenic disturbances. There is a vital need to be able to predict the impacts of these disturbances on ecological communities. Species’ attributes such as habitat preference and functional morphological traits may help in uncovering broad patterns in their responses to anthropogenic habitat disturbance. We examined trait-habitat associations in 251 tropical butterfly species by measuring three morphological traits (body mass, wing length and proboscis length) and classifying species according to their habitat preference (forest, ecotone, open). We then correlated these measures (morphological traits and habitat preference) to responses of butterflies to two common habitat disturbances, i.e., a road passing through forest, and dominance of an invasive plant Lantana camara. Both evolutionary relatedness (i.e., family affiliation) and habitat preference explained considerable variation in butterfly morphological traits, suggesting a relationship between evolutionary relatedness, habitat preference and morphology. Both habitat preference and morphological traits influenced response to habitat disturbance: (a) forest roads were frequented by smaller butterflies (b) Lantana-dominated patches were depauperate in larger butterfly species and species with long probosces that are usually associated with deep-flowered forest plants, and (c) habitat preference was related to disturbance from both road and Lantana, with forest-specialized butterfly species showing a negative response. These results suggest that tropical butterflies show generalized responses to habitat disturbance according to their habitat preference and functional morphological traits.

Response to habitat disturbance: We observed responses of butterflies to two habitat disturbances, viz., a road passing through forest and lantana, through surveys carried out in the Biligiri Rangaswamy Temple (BRT) Tiger Reserve in the Western Ghats (Karnataka, India). Study site is a protected forest criss-crossed with unpaved roads, and heavily invaded with alien plants, primarily lantana. Studies that measured lantana occurrence and density in 1997 (Murali and Setty 2001) and 2007—2008 (Sundaram and Hiremath 2012) report that, at the landscape scale, lantana abundance increased enormously, from being present in 41% of the plots in 1997 to 81% of plots by 2008, while the density of lantana stems per plot increased threefold in the same time (Sundaram and Hiremath 2012). We demarcated a study area of 1 km × 0.3 km in the moist deciduous forest patch of BRT. To measure responses to road and lantana, we surveyed butterfly species along 100 m belt transects in two micro-habitats within the study area, i.e., the road verge $(n = 10 in \text{°W} \text{°W})$ season, i.e., Sep-Oct 2012, n = 7 in “Dry” season, i.e., Feb-Apr 2013) and the forest interior (n = 7 in Wet season and n = 8 in Dry season 2013). The forest interior transects were laid in areas with different levels of lantana cover. Along these interior transects, we quantified lantana extent as percentage cover, by visually estimating the percentage cover of lantana in two 5 m × 5 m plots, laid on each side of the transect every 10 m. We took the mean of these 20 readings to characterize the lantana cover for that transect. We classified transects with lantana cover 25% as “high” lantana (n = 4 in Wet season, and n = 4 in Dry season). We walked each road and interior transect (100 m each) 3–5 times in each season, at a fixed slow pace of 10 min per walk. We obtained species abundance data by noting the identity of every butterfly encountered along the transects. To test associations between traits and response to habitat disturbance, we ran simple linear models, with an index of aversion as the response variable, and each of the traits, i.e., body mass, wing length, proboscis length and habitat preference as individual predictors. In case of road vs. interior, ecotone and ecotone-open species were pooled into a single category, i.e., ecotone-open, due to a smaller number of species in each individual category, thus getting a factor with three levels (ecotone-open: n = 17; forest: n = 17; open: n = 11). In case of aversion to lantana, we pooled ecotone and open species into a single category, i.e., ecotoneopen, since there were relatively few representatives of each

individual category, thus getting a factor with two levels (ecotone-open: n = 14; forest: n = 16). We did not run multi-ple regressions because (a) we wanted to thoroughly explore individual trait-disturbance relationships, and (b) traits were somewhat correlated and hence could not be included in a single model.
